title: A ball
sentences: My dear Eleonora!
I am ill, I lie abed, I am in despair.
Ah, I shall never dance a quadrille again.
I shall become a nun or marry, or kill myself in some other way.
Just imagine what happened to me!
Oh, it is dreadful!
it is terrible!
it is horrible!
you would never read such a thing even in a novel.
You may have heard that last week, after the Battle of Branyiszkó, the Hungarian armies passed through here.
There was panic and uproar everywhere; at the news of their coming we believed they would set the town on fire,
that they would rob and kill us, and Mama even said that far worse might befall us,
and she tried hard to persuade me to blacken my face with soot so that I would be repulsive.
Have you ever heard such a wish?
Before long the Hungarian army marched in to the sound of music.
Papa went out to meet them with the deputation, all the servants ran off to watch the soldiers, and I could not find Mama anywhere in the whole house,
for days she had been racking her brains over where she might hide, and when I called and searched for her she never answered,
and if I happened to find her in the wardrobe or the clock-case she scolded me terribly for giving away her hiding place.
Left alone, I thought it wisest to lay out all sorts of food and wine on the table, so perhaps the Hungarians would not eat me,
if they found better fare, and I resolved that whatever they asked for I would give them and not show that I was afraid of them.
And then I waited in complete resignation for the townspeople to come running through the streets crying for help.
At last I heard spurred footsteps and the clink of swords in the entrance hall, but still no cursing; on the contrary, a very polite double knock at the door.
Whether from fright, embarrassment, or I know not what, I could not bring myself to say the word: come in.
But do not imagine they broke down the door with rifle butts for that;
the knock was repeated, and the door opened only at my word.
I had expected at least six fierce Tartars to come through it, with square heads, shaggy leather caps, beards down to their belts, wrapped in untanned bearskin,

with leather sacks on their backs into which they could pack whatever they pleased, and terrifying with knives and pistols, just as Mama had painted them with prophetic inspiration — but imagine my surprise,
when instead of all that two handsome young officers entered our house, one fair, one dark, and both very well dressed and very neat.
An elegant red-braided dolman was thrown over their shoulders, beneath it a tight fashionable attila,
no bearskin or square heads to be seen; indeed I found one of them a very handsome dark-haired young man.
Their first act was to ask permission for intruding, whereupon I stammered something
to the effect that I did not consider it an intrusion, and that I was ready to serve them with whatever they commanded.
That dark-haired young man, taking my words to refer to the side of bacon and wine bottles set out on the table,
could not suppress an understanding smile, which put me to infinite confusion; I believe I must have blushed deeply,
if he noticed that I had prepared those two hundredweight of bacon for him.
At last the fair officer rescued me from my embarrassment, thanking me in a very gentle, flattering tone for every offer of service,
and asking only that I show them a room where they might rest, for they were very tired,
having not slept in a bed for six weeks and not lain down at all for two days.
Poor boys, I almost felt sorry for them.
Not to sleep in a bed for six weeks!
— And yet, you know, how unpleasant it is to sleep on a sofa or a camp bed — I asked him.
Both of them burst out laughing.
— On the bare ground, in the snow, under the open sky — one of them replied.
Well, look at that!
And they endure it!
Among us even the servants would fall deathly ill if they slept outdoors one winter night.
They must truly be some breed of Tartar.
— Follow me — I said, and led them to our finest room, where there happened to be two beds.
All our servants had gone off from home, and I wanted to make up the beds for them myself.
— Ah, we cannot allow that; we can manage that ourselves —
they said with polite insistence, and seeing that they needed rest, I left them alone.
I had scarcely reached my room when I heard terrible screaming and shouting from theirs.
— Help!
robbers!
murderers!
I knew the voice, but in my fright I could not guess whose it was.
— Robbers, murderers!
help!
If you can put yourself in my place, you may guess that I certainly did not run to the aid of the one shouting,
until she finally burst through the rooms straight to me.
It was dear Mama…
But in what a state!
Her dress crumpled every which way, her cap slipped down over her eyes, she had lost one slipper somewhere, and she was red
as though taken straight from the oven, and she kept shouting and wailing and calling for help.
It took me a long while to find out from her where she had been and what had happened to her.
Well, she had hidden herself in precisely the room where I had lodged the two guests, and indeed under the bottom of the bed, beneath all the bolsters.
Now you can imagine the rest: when that honvéd officer, dead tired, threw himself onto the bed,
poor Mama certainly had reason to cry for help.
But whatever put such an idea into her head?
It cost me great effort to calm Mama somewhat and persuade her that those soldiers had not come here to rob and murder;
I finally brought matters so far that she promised not to hide herself again,
and I would explain to the officers that Mama had rheumatism and had crept under all the bolsters to take a sweating bath.
Hardly had my guests had time to doze off when an orderly came and wanted to speak with them.
— That is impossible — I said — wait, or come back later, for they are asleep.
— Where are they asleep?
— he asked.
I showed him the room, and he, without giving it a moment's thought
whether it was proper to wake a man when he falls asleep for the first time in three days, walked into their room.
I was frightened; I thought the officers would cut this man to pieces for waking them.
But they did not; indeed, a few minutes later both were fully dressed, without the slightest sign of displeasure, and followed the orderly.
The major had sent for them.
Strange, this soldier folk!
How they can obey without a word of objection!
But I would not make a good soldier.
I should always want to know beforehand, when something is commanded, why it was commanded.
Half an hour later our officers returned.
No ill humour, no sign of sleeplessness showed on them; they hardly wished to go back to their room, but came to find Mama and me,
and with flattering joy informed us that this evening the officers' corps would improvise a dance,
and that we too were invited, and they immediately secured my promise for a quadrille, a csárdás, and a polonaise, for there would be no waltz.
Naturally I promised them everything at once.
This was the first dance in our house since the middle of carnival.
They seemed no less pleased than I, for after that they wanted to hear no more of sleep.
But Mama kept tugging at me and raising objections.
— You have no ball gown.
— Of course I do — the white one.
I have worn it only once.
— That is not fashionable.
— Just a little national ribbon on it — interposed my dark officer — and Your Grace will wear the finest fashion of all.
— But my foot hurts — Mama excused herself.
— Your Grace need not dance if you do not wish to, dear Mama.
The officers, out of pure courtesy, did not laugh; Mama, for similar reasons, did not scold them; she only turned on me when they had gone to their room.
— You wretched girl!
This is how you rush headlong into certain ruin!
This is how you throw yourself away of your own free will!
I thought that, as usual when I was preparing for a ball, she was afraid of consumption,
and I thought I would greatly reassure her by reminding her that we would not dance a waltz.
That made her even angrier.
— You have no sense!
Why do they give a ball now — so that they may dance, perhaps?
Of course that is why; it is all finesse, all a plot by the Hungarians,
to lure the town's young girls all into one place and then suddenly carry them off to Turkey.
— Ah, Mama!
Officers are not allowed to marry in wartime — I replied, laughing.
At that she scrubbed my face even harder, called me a silly goose, and said they would not carry us off to make us their wives anyway.
Then I do not know what else men could want us for, if not to marry.
— You shall see — Mama threatened, but she did not hold me back.
Until evening I was busy with preparations.
At my officer's direction I tied a broad red-white-green ribbon around the waist of my white ball gown, leaving both ends hanging long in front,
and pinned simple white and red live roses into my coiffure, which with their green leaves made a true national colour.
Only now did I notice how well these colours suit one another.
The two officers were already waiting for us in full dress; the more gallant of the two paid so many compliments that I could scarcely remember them all.
He could not leave unmentioned that little freckle beneath my lip,
over which everyone had hitherto stumbled with their eyes; I do not know what they find to say about it.
I should not mind if it were where no one would ever see it.
I was forced to hide my confusion with loud laughter.
— No, no, this will all end in tears — Mama muttered half audibly,
yet she kept adjusting and arranging something on me, so that if I were carried off, at least they would find everything in order.
The two officers escorted us to the ballroom.
I was already proud in advance of the effect I would win over the others with my national ribbon and two handsome, dashing escorts.
Between us, I still could not give up the hope
that perhaps all the others really did have square heads, and only we had drawn from the round-headed sort.
But what disappointment and surprise!
Each of my friends had put on at least twice as much national colour as I, and as for the other Hungarian officers,
ah, beside them my two chevaliers servants ranked only among the second- and third-rate stars.
One was more charming, one handsomer than the next, agile, well dressed, attentive; one could scarcely believe they had shed so much blood!
One in particular caught my eye — not only mine, but everyone's.
A beautiful tall, slender honvéd captain.
That little black wreath-beard suited his lovely pale-red face so well; the red-braided attila looked as though cast upon him.
And how he danced!
with what fire he danced the polonaise, the csárdás; one would have liked to rush up and kiss him before the whole world — and I do not speak only for myself.
And what was more than dancing, more than compliments, was the je ne sais quoi in his great dark longing eyes;
you cannot imagine it — it was more than words can describe; it intoxicated, it quickened, it killed and saved.
Within an hour every girl, every woman was mad about him.
I do not except myself.
Well, if they make such conquests on the battlefield too, I do not know whether any fortress will remain untaken before them.
And now imagine my feelings when he once glides over to me and asks me for the next quadrille.
Unhappy me!
I was already promised to another.
How I wished they had suddenly sent my partner off somewhere as a courier!
— Then the one after that — the handsome captain continued to dispute the engagement and sat down beside me.
I do not know whether I said anything to him, but I do know that I felt as though I were flying in a dream.
— But Your Grace will forget that you promised me — he went on teasing me.
If I had not suddenly come to myself, I might have answered that I would sooner forget that I existed in this world.
However, I replied in a sufficiently moderate tone that I would not forget.
— But Your Grace will not recognize me…
Some country goose in my place would have answered: Out of a hundred!
out of a thousand, at first glance!
I did not.
As though doing the most indifferent thing in the world, I took the single rosebud pinned to my bosom,
which had half opened there, and without trying to notice the effect, held it out to him.
— By this I shall know you.
All this in the tone with which the magistrate gives a traveller his passport.
The captain softly pressed the rose to his lips.
I did not look, but I saw nonetheless.
I would not have looked him in the eye for half the world at that moment.
Then he withdrew, sat down beneath a mirror opposite me, and did not dance.
There he fell entirely into a reverie.
Meanwhile two more csárdás dances and one polonaise were danced; only then did my quadrille come up.
You can imagine how long the time seemed to me until then; those endless "three dances" would not come to an end.
Never have I seen people dance so furiously.
And yet this was their third night without sleep, and still they would not grow tired so that my quadrille might have its turn.
Meanwhile I found much amusement by striking up an acquaintance with the battalion commander present, Major Sch.,
a very merry, entertaining man.
He has a German name, speaks Hungarian terribly badly, yet always speaks Hungarian even when addressed in German.
But his most striking trait is that he hears very poorly.
Yes, he is accustomed to speech as loud as the conversation of cannons with one another.
Yet they say he is a very brave soldier.
His figure is not particularly alluring.
Long, thin face and frame; the closely cropped hair and recently grown moustache suit him not at all.
Our amusement was most peculiar: what I said he did not hear, and what he said I did not understand.
He brought me a paper cone filled with bonbons; I complained how poor a confectioner we have in our town.
He, inferring from my expression that someone at the ball had offended me terribly, said something in reply,
and judging from the gesture accompanying his words, nothing less than that he would split the man in two from neck to heel — unless I am to believe
that this man's customary gesture in war is what other men use to express a blow to kill.
At last my quadrille arrived.
The band drew out the introduction, and at that everyone hurried to his partner.
My heart nearly burst the side of my corset, so violently it beat when I saw my partner approaching me; he bowed before me, pressing my flower to his heart.
How hot his hand was when he clasped mine.
I rejoiced, I laughed, I was beside myself.
— Ah, you are stealing my neighbour's partner!
— the major cried to him, laughing (that head-butting gesture truly is his customary one).
And we glided into the dance column.
I believe I heard whispering behind me: "What a well-matched pair."
Ah, Eleonora!
how happy I was; I felt as though through our clasped hands my blood flowed into his and his into mine.
We waited for the music.
But before it could begin, the thunder of galloping horses was heard in the street,
and from afar a few cannon shots whose sound made the windows of the hall tremble.
And in the same instant a man entered the hall, cap on head, splashed with mud, and reported that the enemy had attacked the outposts.
The major heard the cannon fire too, and could read from the courier's face what he had not understood from his words.
— Ah!
that is very well!
— he said, slapping his palm (again with that gesture by which one expresses a man's death).
— We have been expecting them.
Messieurs, beg your ladies' leave for one moment.
Only one moment, mes dames; we shall return at once — keep your seats until then.
And off he went to buckle on his sword.
And the other officers too sprang for their weapons; the gracious, smiling,
flattering faces I saw suddenly turn into angry, daring, threatening ones — not one frightened or trembling.
My partner left me too.
Off he went to buckle on sword and cap.
In each one's stride was more boldness, in each face more courage, in each eye more brilliance; if before I had felt love and delight because of him, now he stirred wonder and devotion in me.
When he had buckled on his sword, a strange heat seized every fibre of my being,
and I almost wished to go into battle with him, ride beside him, encourage him and admire him as he charged among the enemy.
He still held my rose in his hand, and when he put on his cap he pinned it beside his cockade; then he turned back and seemed to search the crowd with his eyes.
Our eyes met.
He hurried away, and all the officers with him.
We, however, remained together as though nothing had happened; the major had ordered that no one leave before his return.
The longest hour of my life I lived through then.
Several of us went to the window to listen, and we watched and reasoned, judging from the cannon thunder sounding nearer or farther away.
No one thought it wise to go home, since it was possible that the two armies might clash in a street battle somewhere.
It was better to wait here together for the outcome of the fight.
Before long the cannon thunder began to move farther and farther away, and finally died out altogether.
The civilians with us inferred from this that the Hungarians had won.
They were right.
Scarcely a quarter of an hour later we heard the officers' corps returning with great clamour and merry noise; they came into the hall, cheerful, jesting, as though nothing had happened,
some still brushing something from their clothes (mud, or blood?), and everyone hurried to find his partner and console her.
— Where did we leave off?
— one asked.
— Yes!
at the quadrille — several said, and began to arrange the columns as though coming from the supper room.
Only my partner was not yet here, nor the major.
I kept staring at the door; someone was constantly coming through it — only not the one I waited for.
At last he came through it — the major.
He looked around, and when he saw me, came over.
He made a strange compliment before me, and without waiting for me to speak, said:
— Fair maiden, your partner begs a thousand pardons through me for his rudeness, in that, despite the best will in the world, he cannot enjoy
the pleasure of dancing the promised contredanse with Your Grace, since his lower leg was shot off in battle and he must have it amputated above the knee…
Ah, Eleonora, I shall never dance a quadrille again.
I am ill, I lie abed, I am in despair.
